---
title: "Coordinate Reference Systems: Why Your Map Looks Wrong"
date: 2026-09-06
categories: [tool, geometry, bilingual]
description: "An interactive lab with Python, R and MapLibre — upload a GeoJSON, find out what CRS it's actually in, spot a CRS that doesn't match its own coordinates, and convert it to a different one."
---

Before a geometry can be invalid, or two features can overlap, a file
has to actually be *where it says it is*. A coordinate reference
system (CRS) is what makes a pair of numbers mean a specific place on
Earth — and it's easy to get wrong in a way that neither
[geometry validity](geometry-validity.qmd) nor
[topology checks](topology-errors.qmd) would ever catch, because both
of those only look at the shape, never at where it actually sits.

Just want to quickly check a file, without the rest of the reading?
Use the [standalone tool](/tools/crs-inspector.html) — same engine,
less prose.

## 1. Upload your file

A `.geojson`, or a shapefile: either as a single `.zip`, or as the
individual `.shp`/`.dbf`/`.shx` files (and optionally `.prj`) selected
together.

## 2. Why a CRS problem is different

A geometry can be perfectly valid, and every feature can be perfectly
consistent with every other, and the whole file can still land
thousands of kilometers from where it should. GeoJSON — and MapLibre,
the map library this whole site draws with — assume every coordinate
is WGS84 (plain longitude/latitude). Neither reprojects anything on
its own: whatever numbers you hand them, that's where they land.

- **CRS** — the coordinate reference system a file *declares* it's
  in, read from its own metadata (a `.prj` file for a shapefile, a
  `crs` object for GeoPandas/`sf`). Some files declare none at all.
- **Geographic vs. projected** — a geographic CRS (WGS84 is the
  common one) uses degrees, roughly -180..180 longitude and -90..90
  latitude. A projected CRS (UTM zones, Web Mercator, national grids)
  uses linear units — usually meters — and the numbers involved are
  routinely in the hundreds of thousands or millions.
- **The mismatch** — a file can declare one kind of CRS while its
  actual coordinate values look like the other. That disagreement is
  the single most common reason a map "looks wrong" before you've
  touched a single geometry.

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #crs-diagnose-py}
#| package: geopandas, shapely
import geopandas as gpd
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

gdf = None
for path in ["/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip"]:
    try:
        gdf = gpd.read_file(path)
        break
    except Exception:
        pass

if gdf is None:
    # Deliberately mismatched: no CRS declared, so GeoPandas assumes
    # WGS84 (per the GeoJSON spec) — but these coordinates are Web
    # Mercator magnitude, not degrees. That disagreement IS the
    # example.
    poly = Polygon([(1390000, 5140000), (1391000, 5140000), (1391000, 5141000), (1390000, 5141000), (1390000, 5140000)])
    gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"name": ["mismatched-example"]}, geometry=[poly])

if "name" not in gdf.columns:
    gdf["name"] = [f"geometry {i+1}" for i in range(len(gdf))]

crs_warning = None
if gdf.crs is None:
    gdf = gdf.set_crs("EPSG:4326")
    crs_warning = "No CRS found in the file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."

original_crs = gdf.crs
is_geographic = bool(original_crs.is_geographic)
bounds = [round(float(b), 6) for b in gdf.total_bounds]

# The actual check: does the CRS's OWN claim (geographic vs projected)
# agree with the magnitude of the coordinates themselves?
looks_geographic = (
    -180 <= bounds[0] <= 180 and -180 <= bounds[2] <= 180 and
    -90 <= bounds[1] <= 90 and -90 <= bounds[3] <= 90
)
mismatch_warning = None
if is_geographic and not looks_geographic:
    mismatch_warning = f"Declared as geographic ({original_crs.name}), but the coordinates are far outside -180..180 / -90..90 — likely actually projected."
elif not is_geographic and looks_geographic:
    mismatch_warning = f"Declared as projected ({original_crs.name}), but the coordinates already look like lon/lat — likely actually geographic."

# MapLibre/GeoJSON require WGS84 — the summary keeps the file's own
# native CRS on purpose (that mismatch is the whole point), so the map
# gets its own throwaway reprojected copy.
map_gdf = gdf if original_crs == "EPSG:4326" else gdf.to_crs("EPSG:4326")

{
    "features": map_gdf.__geo_interface__,
    "summary": {
        "crs": original_crs.to_string(),
        "isGeographic": is_geographic,
        "bounds": bounds,
        "crsWarning": crs_warning,
        "mismatchWarning": mismatch_warning
    }
}
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #crs-diagnose-r}
#| package: sf, geojsonsf, jsonlite
data <- NULL
for (path in c("/uploaded.geojson", "/uploaded.shp", "/vsizip//uploaded.zip")) {
  data <- tryCatch(sf::st_read(path, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(data)) break
}

if (is.null(data)) {
  wkt <- "POLYGON((1390000 5140000, 1391000 5140000, 1391000 5141000, 1390000 5141000, 1390000 5140000))"
  data <- sf::st_sf(name = "mismatched-example", geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(wkt))
}

if (!("name" %in% names(data))) {
  data$name <- paste("geometry", seq_len(nrow(data)))
}

crs_warning <- NULL
if (is.na(sf::st_crs(data))) {
  sf::st_crs(data) <- 4326
  crs_warning <- "No CRS found in the file — assuming WGS84 (EPSG:4326)."
}

original_crs <- sf::st_crs(data)
is_geographic <- sf::st_is_longlat(data)
bnd <- sf::st_bbox(data)
bounds <- unname(round(as.numeric(bnd), 6))

looks_geographic <- (
  bounds[1] >= -180 && bounds[1] <= 180 && bounds[3] >= -180 && bounds[3] <= 180 &&
  bounds[2] >= -90 && bounds[2] <= 90 && bounds[4] >= -90 && bounds[4] <= 90
)
mismatch_warning <- NULL
if (isTRUE(is_geographic) && !looks_geographic) {
  mismatch_warning <- paste0("Declared as geographic (", original_crs$input, "), but the coordinates are far outside -180..180 / -90..90 -- likely actually projected.")
} else if (!isTRUE(is_geographic) && looks_geographic) {
  mismatch_warning <- paste0("Declared as projected (", original_crs$input, "), but the coordinates already look like lon/lat -- likely actually geographic.")
}

map_data <- if (isTRUE(original_crs == sf::st_crs(4326))) data else sf::st_transform(data, 4326)

# jsonlite::unbox() marks a value as a genuine scalar, explicitly,
# field by field — see geospatial-file-inspection.qmd for why this is
# preferred over a blanket auto_unbox flag.
result <- list(
  features = jsonlite::fromJSON(geojsonsf::sf_geojson(map_data), simplifyVector = FALSE),
  summary = list(
    crs = jsonlite::unbox(original_crs$input),
    isGeographic = jsonlite::unbox(is_geographic),
    bounds = bounds,
    crsWarning = if (is.null(crs_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(crs_warning),
    mismatchWarning = if (is.null(mismatch_warning)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(mismatch_warning)
  )
)
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
pyDiagnose = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("crs-diagnose-py", Generators)
{
  if (pyDiagnose) {
    await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("crs-py", pyDiagnose.features);
    // Zooms to whatever was just diagnosed — especially relevant here:
    // the mismatched example's whole point is landing far from the
    // map's fixed initial view. A no-op on an empty FeatureCollection.
    await sharedMap.fitToData(pyDiagnose.features);
    mutable pySummary = pyDiagnose.summary;
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
rDiagnose = WebGeoDS.getCellValue("crs-diagnose-r", Generators)
{
  if (rDiagnose) {
    await sharedMap.setGeoJSON("crs-r", rDiagnose.features);
    await sharedMap.fitToData(rDiagnose.features);
    mutable rSummary = rDiagnose.summary;
  }
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Two summary cards side by side — Python's and R's — same reasoning
// as geospatial-file-inspection.qmd's own statCard: merging two CRS
// strings wouldn't mean anything, seeing them agree (or where they
// diverge in formatting) is itself the point.
statCard = (label, s) => {
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.style.flex = "1";
  wrap.style.minWidth = "260px";

  const heading = document.createElement("div");
  heading.className = "webgeods-label";
  heading.textContent = label;
  wrap.appendChild(heading);

  const box = document.createElement("div");
  box.className = "webgeods-stat-grid";
  wrap.appendChild(box);

  const row = (rowLabel, value) => {
    const dt = document.createElement("div");
    dt.className = "webgeods-stat-label";
    dt.textContent = rowLabel;
    const dd = document.createElement("div");
    dd.className = "webgeods-stat-value";
    dd.textContent = value;
    box.append(dt, dd);
  };

  if (!s) {
    row("CRS", "—");
    return wrap;
  }

  row("CRS", s.crsWarning ? `${s.crs} ⚠️ ${s.crsWarning}` : s.crs);
  row("Type", s.isGeographic ? "Geographic (degrees)" : "Projected (usually meters)");
  row("Bounds", s.bounds.join(", "));
  row(s.mismatchWarning ? "⚠️ Mismatch" : "Mismatch check", s.mismatchWarning ?? "✓ CRS and coordinates agree");

  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
statCardsRow = {
  const row = document.createElement("div");
  row.style.display = "flex";
  row.style.flexWrap = "wrap";
  row.style.gap = "16px";
  row.append(statCard("Python", pySummary), statCard("R", rSummary));
  return row;
}
```

${statCardsRow}

  for (const id of ["crs-py", "crs-r"]) {
    if (sharedMap.getGeoJSON(id)) {
      await sharedMap.setGeoJSON(id, { type: "FeatureCollection", features: [] });
    }

  mutable rSummary = null;
}

## 4. Same spatial question, two languages

Python and R answer "is this CRS geographic or projected?" with one
line each:

**Python**

```python
gdf.crs.is_geographic
```

**R**

```r
sf::st_is_longlat(data)
```

Both ultimately ask PROJ (the library underneath both PyPROJ and
`sf`'s CRS handling) the same question — but the accessor and the
formatted CRS string differ: `original_crs.to_string()` in Python
routinely returns `"EPSG:4326"`, while `st_crs(data)$input` in R
returns whatever string the file's own CRS definition resolved to,
sometimes a full human-readable name instead of an EPSG code. Same
underlying CRS, not always the same displayed text — worth knowing
before assuming a mismatch between the two cards above means an
actual data problem, rather than a formatting one.

## 5. Convert to a different CRS

Once you know the CRS, changing it is one call — `to_crs()` in
GeoPandas, `st_transform()` in `sf`. Reuses exactly the data just
diagnosed above (`gdf` in Python, `data` in R stay in the session
between one cell and the next), no new reading of the file.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Python

```{.webgeods-python #crs-convert-py}
# A common target: Web Mercator (EPSG:3857), the projection most
# online basemap tiles use. Printed as text, not drawn on the shared
# map above — MapLibre/GeoJSON require WGS84, so a genuinely converted
# result (unless the target IS 4326) can't be shown there directly.
converted = gdf.to_crs("EPSG:3857")
f"{len(converted)} feature(s) now in {converted.crs.to_string()}, bounds {[round(b, 2) for b in converted.total_bounds]}"
```

## R

```{.webgeods-r #crs-convert-r}
converted <- sf::st_transform(data, 3857)
sprintf("%d feature(s) now in %s, bounds %s", nrow(converted), sf::st_crs(converted)$input, paste(round(as.numeric(sf::st_bbox(converted)), 2), collapse = ", "))
```

:::

::: {.callout-note}
Converting *to* a CRS is only correct when the CRS you're converting
*from* is right in the first place. If the mismatch check above found
a problem, `to_crs()`/`st_transform()` would mathematically transform
numbers that were never really in the declared CRS to begin with,
producing a confident-looking but wrong result — fixing the file's own
CRS label (something only you can determine, from where the data
actually came from) has to come first.
:::

## 6. Where to next

- **Geometry looks fine, dataset doesn't?** →
  [Topology errors](topology-errors.qmd) covers overlaps, gaps,
  slivers, duplicates and dangles — relationships *between* features,
  a different problem from CRS entirely.
- **Not sure where to start?** → The
  [GeoSpatial File Inspector](geospatial-file-inspection.qmd) gives a
  five-second summary of a file — feature count, geometry type, CRS,
  bounds, attributes — before you dig into any one check.
- **Just needed the check?** → The
  [standalone CRS Inspector & Converter](/tools/crs-inspector.html)
  runs the same detection and lets you convert and download directly.
